title: Planting for pollinators, even in a pot
description: Bees and butterflies need flowers across the seasons, and a single pot or window box can be part of that chain.

body.heading: Why small plantings count
paragraphs: Pollinators travel surprising distances between food sources, and a neighbourhood dotted with flowering pots, window boxes and garden corners works like a chain of cafés along their route. Your one pot matters most as part of that chain, which is a comforting thought.
Flowers also feed the insects that birds eat and that gardens quietly depend on, so a pot of blooms supports far more life than the bees you actually see.

body.heading: Choose flowers they can use
paragraphs: Simple, open flowers are easiest for bees and butterflies to feed from; heavily doubled blooms, bred for looks, often hide or remove the nectar and pollen entirely. Herbs like thyme, oregano and lavender, left to flower, are pollinator favourites that also earn their keep in the kitchen.
Aim for a sequence across the year rather than one glorious week: something for early spring, something for high summer, and something still flowering into autumn, when food grows scarce.

body.heading: Skip the sprays, add some water
paragraphs: Avoid insecticides on flowering plants, since they harm the very visitors you are feeding. A shallow dish of water with a few pebbles as landing spots is a small kindness on hot days.
If a pot is all you can manage, manage it proudly. A balcony rail of flowers in a street of bare concrete can be the busiest feeding station on the road.

takeaway: Open flowers across the seasons, no sprays, a dish of water: even one pot becomes a service station for pollinators.
